title: Landers and Telegram
summary: How to build the pages and Telegram spaces that sit between your ad and the offer: prelanders, quizzes, honest advertorials, channels, groups, join requests, bots, welcome flows and broadcasts. A good funnel warms people up honestly and keeps working the lead for weeks after the click. It ends with building and wiring your own lander so every click ID reaches the offer and every page test can be judged with the starting rules.

lessons.title: Prelanders that earn the click
objectives: By the end you can explain what a prelander does and when to skip one
By the end you can choose between a bridge page, listicle, calculator and VSL
By the end you can build a fast, mobile-first prelander with one clear action
By the end you can work out whether a prelander is paying for itself
By the end you can apply the starting rule card to a direct link vs prelander test

steps.p: A prelander is a short page between your ad and the offer page. Its job is to take a cold person who tapped an ad in two seconds and give them enough context to take the next step on purpose. It does not close the sale. It prepares the reader for the offer.
steps.say: Think of a prelander as a bridge. It's a short page that sits between your ad and the offer page. Someone tapped your ad in two seconds, so they arrive cold. The prelander's job is to give them just enough context to take the next step on purpose. Notice what it doesn't do. It doesn't close the sale. It warms the reader up, then hands them over to the offer.

steps.p: Sending people straight to the offer is simpler and loses fewer clicks. A prelander loses some clicks but can send better-prepared people forward. Which wins depends on the offer and the audience, so you test both.

a.title: Direct link
items: Offer page does all the work

b.title: Prelander
items: Good for new or complex offers
You own the page and the data

steps.say: Here's the big choice, side by side. On the left, the direct link. Fewer steps, fewer drop-offs, and the offer page does all the work, which suits simple, known products. On the right, the prelander. It adds one extra step, so you lose some clicks, but you get to explain the offer first, and you own the page and the data. Which one wins depends on the offer and the audience. That's why you test both.

steps.p: Most prelanders fall into a few shapes. Pick the one that matches what the reader needs to understand before the offer makes sense to them.
d: Calculator|reader enters numbers, sees a result
VSL|a short explainer video above the button
steps.say: Most prelanders fall into one of four shapes, shown on these cards. A bridge page is a short intro with one button. A listicle gives ranked tips or options. A calculator lets the reader enter numbers and see a result. And a V S L, a video sales letter, puts a short explainer video above the button. Pick the format that matches what the reader needs to understand before the offer makes sense.

steps.h: The shape of a page that works
steps.p: Good prelanders follow the same order. A headline that matches the ad, a short problem, the honest answer, proof that is real, then one button. Anything that does not move the reader down this line gets cut.
steps.say: Good prelanders follow the same order. Follow the line on screen. First, a headline that matches the ad. Then a short statement of the problem. Then the honest answer. Then proof that is real. And finally, one button. Here's the useful test: anything on the page that doesn't move the reader down this line gets cut.

steps.h: Message match is the first test
steps.p: If the ad says 'Learn to read a trading chart in 10 minutes' and the page opens with 'Join the best broker', the reader feels tricked and leaves. Repeat the ad's promise, in the ad's words, in the first line of the page.

d.text: Read the ad, then read only the page headline. If they do not sound like one conversation, rewrite the headline.

steps.p: Every second of loading costs you readers who already paid you a click. The figures below are an illustration of the pattern, not a benchmark. Measure your own page.
steps.say: Every second of loading costs you readers who already paid you a click. Look at the bars. These are illustration figures, not a benchmark. In this example, a page loading in one and a half seconds keeps ninety percent of people. At three seconds, seventy percent. At six seconds, forty five percent. At ten seconds, only twenty five percent stay. The pattern is what matters. Measure your own page.

steps.p: A prelander has its own numbers, separate from the ad and the offer. Track them per page version so you know whether the page helps or hurts. If load rate is low, fix speed. If page CTR is low, fix the message. If offer CR is low, the page may be sending the wrong people.
steps.say: A prelander has its own numbers, separate from the ad and the offer. In the table: load rate is page views divided by ad clicks. Click through is button clicks divided by page views. Offer C R, conversion rate, is conversions divided by button clicks. And time on page. Track them per page version. If load rate is low, fix speed. If page C T R, click through rate, is low, fix the message. If offer C R is low, the page may be sending the wrong people.

steps.h: Does the page pay for itself
steps.p: Compare the conversions per 1,000 ad clicks with and without the prelander. The page only stays if it produces more conversions from the same paid clicks.
steps.say: So does the page pay for itself? Here's the equation on screen. Ad clicks, times load rate, times page click through, times offer conversion rate, equals conversions. Compare conversions per thousand ad clicks with and without the prelander. The page only stays if it produces more conversions from the same paid clicks. Not more page clicks. More conversions.

steps.p: Example: 1,000 ad clicks. Direct link: 1,000 × 90% load × 3% offer CR = 27 sign-ups. Prelander: 1,000 × 85% load × 40% page CTR × 10% offer CR = 34 sign-ups. The prelander wins here because it sends fewer but better-prepared people.
steps.more: If the same prelander only lifted offer CR to 6%, you would get 1,000 × 85% × 40% × 6% = about 20 sign-ups, and the direct link would win. That is why you test both versions with the same ad and budget split evenly, and why you look at the final conversion, not the page CTR alone. A page with a high CTR that sends curious but unready people can still lose.

d.text: Direct: 27 sign-ups. Prelander: 34 sign-ups. Same 1,000 clicks. Example figures.

steps.say: Let's work an example. These are example figures. One thousand ad clicks. Direct link: a thousand, times ninety percent load, times three percent offer conversion, gives twenty seven sign-ups. Prelander: a thousand, times eighty five percent load, times forty percent page click through, times ten percent offer conversion, gives thirty four sign-ups. The prelander wins here because it sends fewer but better-prepared people. But if it only lifted offer conversion to six percent, you'd get about twenty, and the direct link would win. So judge the final conversion, not page click through alone.

steps.h: Lab: where does this prelander leak?
steps.p: Use the funnel lab on a prelander's own numbers. Work out the pass-through rate at each step and pick the weakest one. That step is where you work first: speed, message or audience.
steps.more: Working. Loads 850 ÷ 1,000 = 85%. Button 340 ÷ 850 = 40%. Sign-ups 34 ÷ 340 = 10%. The weakest step is sign-up on the offer page. Before blaming the offer, check that the prelander sets honest expectations, because a page that over-promises sends people who leave at the sign-up form.

steps.h: Starting rule for a prelander test
steps.p: Run the direct link and the prelander as two ad sets with the same ad, audience and budget. Apply the starting rule card to each on network-confirmed conversions. Keep the version with the lower CPA once both have spent 3 × target. Adapt to your data.

d.text: Example: target $20. Both spent $60. Direct: 2 sign-ups, $30 CPA, hold at best. Prelander: 4 at $15 CPA, under 0.8 × target, so keep it and allow a +20% step.

Same ad, because otherwise you're testing the ad, not the page. steps.p: Proof builds trust only when it is true. Readers in trading and betting have seen many fake screenshots and they spot them. Fake proof also breaks ad policies and, in many countries, consumer law. Use proof a reader could check for themselves.

b.title: Use instead
items: Plain steps of how it works

steps.say: Proof only builds trust when it's true. Readers in trading and betting have seen plenty of fake screenshots, and they spot them. Fake proof also breaks ad policies and, in many countries, consumer law. On the left, never use: invented testimonials, stock photos posing as users, fake earnings screenshots, or celebrity faces without permission. On the right, use instead: real reviews with permission, licence and regulator details, plain steps of how it works, and clear risk warnings. Use proof a reader could check for themselves.

steps.p: Most prelanders that lose money make one of these mistakes. Each one is cheap to check before launch and expensive to discover after a week of spend.

a.title: Mistakes
items: Heavy images on slow mobile data

b.title: Fixes
items: Compress, test on a cheap phone

steps.say: Most prelanders that lose money make one of these mistakes, each matched to a fix. A headline that ignores the ad, fix it by repeating the ad's promise first. Heavy images on slow mobile data, compress and test on a cheap phone. Three buttons and a pop-up, go to one action per page. Judging by page click through, judge on conversions per thousand clicks instead. And no risk or sponsored label, put labels near the top. Each is cheap to check before launch, and expensive to discover after a week of spend.

steps.h: Same page for everyone, honest labels
steps.p: Every visitor, including ad reviewers, must see the same page. Showing reviewers one page and users another is cloaking, which breaks every major ad policy. On trading and betting pages, show the risk warning and a sponsored label near the top.

options: Close the sale on its own
Hide the offer from ad reviewers
Prepare a cold reader to take the next step on purpose
Collect as many emails as possible

Why most people fail at life

options: A stock photo labelled as a real customer
The broker's regulator and licence number
A screenshot of earnings you made up
A celebrity photo you found online

Turn off tracking and test again
Page CTR and sign-ups mean the same thing
The direct link wins on the number that matters
quiz.why: The final conversion per paid click is what pays you. A high page CTR can send curious but unready people forward.

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll learn what a prelander is, when it helps, and when you should skip it. A prelander can make a campaign or quietly drain it, so knowing how to test one properly matters.
lessons.say_outro: So, a prelander is a bridge that earns its place only if it produces more conversions from the same paid clicks, and it must be fast, honest and clearly labelled. lessons.title: Quizzes and honest advertorials
objectives: By the end you can design a short quiz funnel that segments people honestly
By the end you can write an advertorial that is clearly labelled as advertising
By the end you can spot fake news-style pages, fake scarcity and fake endorsements and avoid them

By the end you can pass a quiz segment and click ID forward to your bot

steps.p: A quiz funnel asks the reader three to five short questions before showing a result and a next step. People like tapping answers more than reading walls of text, and you learn who they are. Used honestly, a quiz both warms people up and sorts them.
steps.say: A quiz funnel asks the reader three to five short questions before showing a result and a next step. Why does that work? People like tapping answers more than reading walls of text. And while they tap, you learn who they are. Used honestly, a quiz does two jobs at once. It warms people up, and it sorts them, so you can guide each one properly.

steps.p: Keep a quiz funnel short. Every extra question loses a few readers, so each question must change what you show or send at the end. If an answer would not change the result or the follow-up, remove that question.
steps.say: Keep a quiz funnel short. Follow the shape on screen: a hook question, then two to four profile questions, then an honest result, then a matched next step. Every extra question loses a few readers, so each one has to earn its place. Here's the test. If an answer wouldn't change the result or the follow-up, remove that question.

steps.p: A quiz that tells everyone they 'qualify' or have 'won' is a trick, and readers feel it the moment they reach the offer. Results must follow from the answers, must not promise outcomes, and must be shown before you ask for anything.

a.title: Rigged
items: Asks for a deposit to 'see results'

b.title: Honest
items: Explains the next step and its risk
Only asks what you will use

steps.say: Now compare an honest result with a rigged one. A quiz that tells everyone they qualify or have won is a trick, and readers feel it the moment they hit the offer. Rigged quizzes promise profit or winnings, ask for a deposit to see results, and collect data with no reason. Honest ones make the result depend on the answers, explain the next step and its risk, show the result before any sign-up, and only ask what you'll use.

steps.p: Measure the drop at each question over at least a few hundred starts. Starting rule: rewrite or remove any question that loses more than twice the average drop of the others. Judge the whole quiz on cost per paid event, not completion rate.

d.text: Example: questions lose 8%, 10% and 40%. Average of the others is 9%; 40% is far over 18%, so rewrite that question first.

Then rewrite or remove any question that loses more than twice the average drop of the others. In the example, questions lose eight, ten and forty percent. The average of the others is nine percent, so the line is eighteen. Forty is far over it, so rewrite that question first. And judge the whole quiz on cost per paid event, not completion rate.

steps.p: These mistakes make quiz funnels lose readers or lose the value of the answers. Most are fixed by cutting questions and using every answer you collect.

a.title: Mistakes
items: Eight questions when four would do
Asking for a phone number before the result

b.title: Fixes
items: Every answer changes the result or follow-up
Pass a segment tag to the next step

steps.say: These mistakes make quizzes lose readers, or lose the value of the answers. Eight questions when four would do, use three to five tap questions. Questions that change nothing, make every answer change the result or follow-up. No progress bar, show progress on every screen. Answers never passed forward, pass a segment tag to the next step. And asking for a phone number before the result, show the result first, then ask.

steps.p: An advertorial is advertising written in the style of an article. It can be useful: it has room to explain a product, its risks and how it works. It becomes dishonest the moment it pretends to be independent news.
steps.say: Now the second style. An advertorial is advertising written in the style of an article. It can be genuinely useful, because it has room to explain a product, its risks and how it works. But it becomes dishonest the moment it pretends to be independent news. The rule is in the subtitle: an ad that explains, always labelled as an ad.

steps.p: These rules keep you inside ad policies on Meta, TikTok and Google, inside consumer and advertising law in most countries, and they keep readers' trust.
steps.more: Advertising regulators exist in most of your geos, for example ARCON in Nigeria and the Advertising Regulatory Board in South Africa, and many have rules on disclosure and on financial or gambling ads. In the EU, UK and US, consumer protection agencies treat disguised advertising as deceptive. Rules change and differ by country; check the current rules for each geo before you run.
d: Your own brand name, not a copy of a news site
No real journalist names or bylines you made up
Claims you can prove, with risks stated
Disclosure if you earn a commission
steps.say: Here are the rules for an honest advertorial. An advertisement or sponsored label at the top. Your own brand name, not a copy of a news site. No real journalist names, and no bylines you made up. Claims you can prove, with risks stated. And disclosure if you earn a commission. These keep you inside ad policies on Meta, TikTok and Google, inside consumer and advertising law in most countries, and they keep readers' trust. Rules differ by country, so check each geo before you run.

steps.p: Some prelander styles are common in the industry and still wrong. They get ad accounts banned and they mislead people who trusted you with a click.

a.title: Fake and banned
items: Copy of BBC, Punch or CNN layout
Countdown timer that resets on reload

b.title: Honest alternative
items: No comments, or real moderated ones

steps.say: Some prelander styles are common in the industry and still wrong. On the left, fake and banned: a copy of a B B C, Punch or C N N layout, a fake celebrity interview, an invented comments section, and a countdown timer that resets on reload. On the right, the honest alternatives: your own clean brand, a real customer story with consent, no comments or real moderated ones, and a real deadline or no deadline. The fakes get accounts banned and mislead people who trusted you.

steps.p: 'Only 3 spots left' on a page anyone can join is a lie. If a limit is real, such as a webinar seat cap or a bonus that ends on a date set by the advertiser, say exactly what it is and when it ends.

d.text: If you cannot prove the limit or deadline exists, delete it.

steps.say: Fake scarcity is still fake. Only three spots left, on a page anyone can join, is a lie. The warning box puts it simply: if you can't prove the limit or deadline exists, delete it.

steps.p: A channel is a broadcast: admins post, members read. A group is a conversation: members can talk to each other. Many operators run both, a channel for content and a linked group for questions.
steps.more: Telegram's limits change from time to time. At the time of writing, groups hold up to 200,000 members and channels have no subscriber limit. A channel can link a discussion group so each post gets a comments thread. Check Telegram's current FAQ for limits before you plan around them.

a.title: Channel
items: Members do not see each other

steps.say: Let's start with the basic choice. A channel is a broadcast: admins post, members read. A group is a conversation: members can talk to each other. On screen, channels have no member limit, members don't see each other, and comments only come through a linked discussion group. Groups let members post, hold up to two hundred thousand members at the time of writing, and need active moderation. Many operators run both, a channel for content and a linked group for questions. Limits change, so check Telegram's current F A Q.

steps.p: Choose by what the reader needs to do, not by habit or by what a competitor uses. If they need to read, use a channel. If they need to ask and talk, use a group. If they need a personal reply, use a bot.
steps.say: So which one for which job? Choose by what the reader needs to do, not by habit or what a competitor uses. A channel for daily posts, education and updates. A group for questions, support and peer chat. A channel plus a group for content with comments. And a bot for a one-to-one welcome and follow-up. The simple rule: to read, a channel. To ask and talk, a group. For a personal reply, a bot.

steps.p: A public channel or group has a @username and a t.me link anyone can find in search. A private one is reachable only through invite links you create. For paid traffic, private with tracked invite links gives you far more control.

a.title: Public
items: Hard to tell which ad brought whom

b.title: Private

For paid traffic, private with tracked invite links gives you far more control.

steps.h: Setting up a channel for paid traffic
steps.p: A clean setup makes the first visit feel trustworthy. It also helps your ads pass review when they mention the channel, because reviewers may open the link. Do these before you send paid traffic.

Description with who you are and a risk note

steps.say: Before you send paid traffic, set the channel up cleanly. A clear name and photo, with no impersonation. A description of who you are, with a risk note. A pinned start-here post. A clean setup makes the first visit feel trustworthy, and it helps your ads pass review, because reviewers may open the link.

steps.h: A bot is your one-to-one line
steps.p: A channel talks to everyone at once. A bot talks to one person at a time, in a private chat, with messages that can depend on who they are and what they did. It is how you welcome, answer and follow up at scale.
steps.say: A channel talks to everyone at once. A bot talks to one person at a time, in a private chat. And its messages can depend on who that person is and what they did. That's what makes it so useful. It's how you welcome, answer and follow up at scale. As the screen says: one chat per person. Automated, personal, and permission-based.

steps.h: What bots can and cannot do
steps.p: Bots are useful but Telegram limits them to protect users from spam. Build your flows within these limits from day one. The limits can change with Bot API updates, so check the official docs before you design a new flow.
steps.more: The usual rule is that a bot can only start a private conversation after the user has opened it and pressed Start, or sent it a message. The join request exception lets a bot message a requester briefly while the request is pending. If a user blocks the bot, sends fail with an error, which is also your best signal that someone has opted out.

steps.p: A bot token works like a password to your bot. If someone else gets it, they can message all your bot users as you, and change what the bot does. Protect it as carefully as your ad account login.
d: Keep the token in a server secret, never in page code
Give the bot only the admin rights it needs
Revoke and replace the token if leaked
steps.say: Finally, bot safety basics. A bot token works like a password to your bot. If someone else gets it, they can message all your bot users as you, and change what the bot does. So keep the token in a server secret, never in page code. Give the bot only the admin rights it needs. Rate-limit your own sends. Log errors and blocks. And revoke and replace the token if it leaks. Protect it as carefully as your ad account login.

lessons.title: Broadcasts, drips and retention

steps.p: A broadcast goes to many people at the same moment. A drip goes to each person on their own timeline, counted from when they joined or acted. You need both.
steps.say: First, two kinds of sending. A broadcast goes to many people at the same moment: same message, same time, for news, live sessions and updates. It's easy to overdo. A drip goes to each person on their own timeline, counted from when they joined or acted. It's for onboarding and education, sent as bot private messages, and it stops when the person acts. You need both.

steps.p: Too few posts and people forget why they joined. Too many and they mute the channel or leave. Start with a modest rhythm, watch your leave rate after each post, and adjust slowly from there.
d: One to three channel posts a day
No posting at 2 a.m. in their time zone
steps.say: Now a posting rhythm that holds. Too few posts and people forget why they joined. Too many and they mute or leave. The checklist gives a starting point: one to three channel posts a day, one clear topic per post, a pinned start-here post, fixed times members can expect, and no posting at two in the morning in their time zone. Start modest, watch your leave rate after each post, and adjust slowly.

steps.p: A mix of post types keeps people reading. Promotion works best when most of your posts are useful on their own, so that members open your messages because they expect something worth their time.
d: Show|a real example or case study

Members open your messages because they expect something worth their time.

steps.h: Retention without and with a plan
steps.p: Illustration: the share of one week's joins still in the channel over 30 days. A steady rhythm and an onboarding drip keep more people. Every member you keep is one you do not have to pay for again.

steps.p: Track these numbers per weekly join cohort, so a good week is not hidden inside a bad month. Comparing cohorts is how you learn whether a change you made actually helped.
steps.more: A cohort is everyone who joined in the same period, usually a week. Comparing cohorts shows whether a change you made, such as a new welcome flow or a new posting time, actually helped. If one post makes leaves jump far above your normal rate, look at what that post said.
steps.say: Here are the retention numbers, all example values. Day seven retention, those still in on day seven divided by those who joined, seventy eight percent. Leave rate per post, leaves within an hour divided by members, point two percent. Bot block rate, blocks divided by bot users, six percent. And F T D, first time deposit, by day thirty, three point five percent. Track these per weekly join cohort, everyone who joined in the same week, so a good week isn't hidden in a bad month.

steps.p: Write these next to your posting plan. They protect the channel the same way the rule card protects ad spend. Starting rules; adapt them to your own normal rates.

If the bot block rate on a send is over two times normal, pause the sequence and check segment and copy. For people inactive fourteen days or more, a maximum of two reactivation messages, then stop. steps.p: Broadcast mistakes rarely show in one day. They show as a slowly shrinking channel and a rising block rate, which means you pay again for people you already had.

steps.p: Small daily habits decide whether your channel compounds or leaks over months. Most of the difference comes from respecting the reader: sending fewer, better messages to the right people and stopping when asked.

steps.h: A lander that loses the click ID loses money
steps.p: If your lander does not pass tracking forward, every sign-up after it arrives with no source. You cannot tell which ad set made money, so you cannot apply a single kill or scale rule. Building the page is easy; wiring it is what pays.

d.b: Build it, wire it, then test it

steps.say: Here's the hard truth on screen. A lander that loses the click I D loses money. If your page doesn't pass tracking forward, every sign-up after it arrives with no source. You can't tell which ad set made money, so you can't apply a single kill or scale rule. Building the page is easy. Wiring it is what pays. So the order is: build it, wire it, then test it.

steps.p: The ad sends a click with campaign names and a click ID. The lander copies them into the offer link. The network sends the conversion back by postback, and your tracker joins it to the ad. Every arrow must carry the IDs.
steps.say: Look at this map of what travels through your lander. The Meta ad sends a click with U T M campaign names and a click I D to your lander. The lander copies them into the offer link as sub values. The offer sign-up produces an F T D, a first time deposit, at the network. The network sends a postback with the click I D to your tracker. And the tracker feeds F T Ds per ad set into your decision sheet. Every arrow must carry the I Ds.

steps.p: Test two versions as two ad sets with the same ad and audience. Each needs about 3 × target to reach the kill and CPA checks. Example: target $20, so $60 per version and $120 for the test.

steps.h: The rule card for each version

Scale twenty percent with three or more conversions, C P A at or under point eight times target, sixteen dollars, and forty eight hours since the last step. Anything else, hold and change nothing. Adapt to your data.

quiz.q: How do you check your ID-copying script works?
options: Open the page with test parameters and inspect the button link
quiz.why: A test click with known values shows straight away whether the button carries sub1 and sub4.

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll build a simple lander and, more importantly, wire it so tracking survives from the ad to the offer. Without that, you can't tell which ad set made money, and you can't run a fair test.
lessons.say_outro: A lander only pays when it's fast, honest, and carries the click I D and campaign names all the way to the offer, so you can test versions fairly with the rule card. Your task: publish one prelander with the I D-copying script, open it on your phone with test values, and confirm the button link carries sub one and sub four. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: You run 1,000 clicks direct to an offer at 3% CR. A prelander test gives 85% load, 35% page CTR and 8% offer CR. Which wins?
exam.why: Direct: 30. Prelander: 1,000 × 0.85 × 0.35 × 0.08 ≈ 24. The direct link wins on final conversions.

exam.q: A teammate builds a prelander that copies a national newspaper's logo and layout, labelled 'Sponsored' in small grey text. What do you do?
options: Rebuild it on your own brand with a clear label
Run it; the label covers it
Run it only in one geo
Remove the label so it looks natural
exam.why: Copying a real outlet impersonates it even with a label. Use your own brand and a clear disclosure.

exam.q: Your quiz tells 100% of people 'You qualify for the VIP program'. What is wrong?
options: The result does not depend on answers and misleads
exam.why: An everyone-qualifies result is a trick. Results must follow from the answers.

exam.q: Which setup lets you see which ad set brought each Telegram join?
options: One public @username link in every ad
A named private invite link per ad set
Asking members which ad they saw
Posting the link in the channel description
exam.why: Separate named links per ad set let you count joins per campaign.

exam.q: You create a bot to approve join requests. Which setup is correct?
options: Username without 'bot', token in the lander code
Bot added as channel admin with permission to invite users, token kept on the server
Bot not added to the channel, approvals by hand
Token shared in the team group for convenience
exam.why: The bot needs admin rights to invite users to approve requests, and the token must stay secret on the server.

exam.q: Ad set A: $200, 800 joins, 20 FTDs. Ad set B: $200, 400 joins, 28 FTDs. Which do you scale?
exam.why: A: $10 per FTD. B: about $7.14 per FTD. Deposits pay you, not joins.

exam.q: Your lander's offer button has a fixed link. Sign-ups arrive in the network report with empty sub IDs. What is the fix?
options: Add a script or tracker that copies the click ID and campaign names into the button link, then test it
Ask the network to guess the source
exam.why: The IDs must travel from the ad, through the lander, into the offer link, or conversions cannot be matched to ad sets.

exam.q: A broadcast to 50,000 bot users is planned. What do you plan for?
options: Using several bots to bypass limits
Queueing within Telegram's rate limits and handling blocked users
exam.why: Respect rate limits, queue sends and treat blocks as opt-outs.

exam.q: A/B lander test, target $20, payout $28. Version A: $65 spent, 2 network sign-ups. Version B: $62 spent, 4 sign-ups. What do the starting rules say?
options: Kill A (CPA $32.50 over the $28 kill line); B at $15.50 CPA qualifies for a +20% step
exam.why: Both spent over 3 × target. A's CPA is above the lower of $30 and $28. B's CPA is under 0.8 × $20 = $16 with 4 conversions.

exam.q: Which line is acceptable on a trading prelander?
options: Only 2 spots left today (no limit exists)
As seen on CNN (it was not)
Trading involves risk. Only use money you can afford to lose.
exam.why: A clear risk warning is honest and often required. The others are false claims or fake scarcity.
